newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says its Burundi rights investigator will stay.
newsitem.headline: UN says its Burundi rights investigator will stay.

text.p: The United Nations insisted on Friday it would not withdraw its human rights envoy from Burundi, after the troubled African country demanded his replacement.

U.N. spokeswoman Therese Gastaut said the United Nations had rejected a demand by Burundi's foreign minister Luc Rukingama for Paulo Sergio Pinheiro, assigned to the job for the past two years, to be replaced.
"We will continue to press for our special rapporteurs to be in a position to visit the countries they have been appointed to monitor," Gastaut told a news briefing.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has given in to demands by Laurent Kabila, leader of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for the replacement of Chilean Roberto Garreton as special U.N. rapporteur probing alleged massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees by Kabila's rebels in the former Zaire.
Garreton angered the Congo ruler by releasing two critical reports of massacres by his followers based on eyewitnesses. Rights groups warned his replacement would set a precedent.
Rukingama has accused Pinheiro, a leading Brazilian human rights authority, of producing slanted reports based on unproven allegations, diplomats said.

Gastaut said Ralph Zacklin, the Geneva-based acting rights chief, had rejected Burundi's demand in a July 16 letter saying the U.N. Human Rights Commission had decided on the investigators' mandates and nominations and that no changes could be made.
Zacklin also asked Burundi to allow a visit by Pinheiro.
"The situation in Burundi is serious and we will continue to press on Burundi to accept the visit of Pinheiro," Gastaut said.

More than 200,000 civilians have been ordered into camps guarded by troops since the army, dominated by ethnic Tutsis, grabbed power in a coup last year. The military says the camps protect people against attacks by ethnic Hutu rebels.
Pinheiro said in March authorities were "systematically resettling rural populations using an outdated strategy of forced villagization".
Rwanda too lobbied intensively in Geneva in April for the U.N. Human Rights Commission not to renew the mandate of a special U.N. rights investigator assigned to the country.
In a resulting compromise seen by diplomats as a downgrading of the key rights post, the body did not renew the envoy's mandate and instead appointed a new rights official to Rwanda.
